title: The Web Origin Concept
summary: Defines the idea of an origin, used by browsers as the unit of authority and isolation, so content from one site cannot interfere with another. It explains how to work out the origin of a URI and write it as a string. It also defines the HTTP Origin header, which shows where a request came from.

plainLanguage.summary: A web origin is the identity of a site for security purposes: the kind of address, the machine, and the port. Two pages have the same origin when all three match, and only content from the same origin may normally read another origin's data. This RFC defines that rule and the HTTP header that reports it.

questions: what makes two urls same origin
what does the origin header contain
why is the scheme part of an origin
subtitle: What a web origin is, how a browser works out the origin of an address, and the Origin header that reports it.

tldr.problem: A browser runs code from many different sites at once, so it needs a way to decide which sites may read each other's data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an origin as the triple of scheme, host and port, explains how to compute the origin of a URI, how to write it as a string, and defines the HTTP Origin header that tells a server which origins caused a request.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard on the standards track, and it registers the Origin header field with IANA.

facts.label: Origin comparison
facts.value: Two origins are the same if and only if they are identical

facts.label: ASCII serialization
facts.value: Scheme, then ://, then the host, then the port if it is not the default

facts.label: Host case folding
facts.value: Lower case, using the i;ascii-casemap collation

today: RFC 6454 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It registers the Origin header field with IANA, as applicable to http, with the IETF as the change controller.

sections.title: Why the Web Needs Origins
sections.content:
User agents interact with content created by a large number of authors. Although many of those authors are well meaning, some might be malicious, and to the extent that user agents take actions based on the content they process, the people who build user agents may wish to restrict the ability of malicious authors to disrupt the confidentiality or integrity of other content or servers.

The example the RFC gives is an HTTP user agent that renders HTML from various servers. If it executes the scripts in those documents, the implementer might want to prevent a script from a malicious server reading documents stored on an honest server, which might for example be behind a firewall.

Traditionally, user agents have divided content according to its origin: content retrieved from one origin may interact freely with other content from that origin, while its interaction with content from another origin is restricted. This document describes the principles behind the same-origin policy, and the practical details of comparing and serializing origins. It does not describe every facet of the policy, because the details are often specific to the application and are left to specifications such as HTML and WebSockets.
sections.plainLanguage: A browser has to run code from thousands of sites at once, and most of those sites are strangers. Origins are the rule that says which strangers are allowed to see each other's data.

sections.title: What an Origin Is
sections.content:
The same-origin policy specifies trust by URI. An HTML document that includes a script with src="https://example.com/library.js" grants the script all of its own privileges, so it declares that it trusts the integrity of what comes from that URI. A form that posts to https://example.com/login exports its secret data to that URI, declaring that it trusts the confidentiality of what is sent there.

In principle a user agent could treat every URI as a separate protection domain and ask for consent whenever content from one URI touched another, but that is cumbersome, because web applications often consist of several resources working together. Instead, user agents group URIs into protection domains called origins. Two URIs are part of the same origin, that is, represent the same principal, if they have the same scheme, host and port.

The RFC explains why each part is there. Including the scheme is essential: without it there would be no isolation between http://example.com and https://example.com, since they share a host, and an active network attacker could corrupt content from the first and have it instruct the user agent to compromise the second, bypassing the protection that TLS gives. The fully qualified host name is used rather than the top-level domain because the trust relationships between host names vary by deployment: at many educational institutions a student can host content at https://example.edu/~student/, but that does not mean such a page should share an origin with a grades application at https://grades.example.edu/. That said, grouping by origin does not always fit a deployment, and the granularity of an origin is in some sense a historical artifact of how the security model evolved.

So http://example.com/, http://example.com:80/ and http://example.com/path/file all have the same origin, while http://example.com:8080/, http://www.example.com/, https://example.com:80/, https://example.com/, http://example.org/ and http://ietf.org/ each have a different one from the others, because in each case at least one of the scheme, host and port components differs.
sections.plainLanguage: An origin is three things: the kind of address, the name of the machine, and the port. The scheme is part of it so that a page fetched over plain HTTP cannot touch one fetched over HTTPS, and the whole host name is part of it so that a student's page is not the same as the university's.

sections.title: Authority Within an Origin
sections.content:
Although user agents group URIs into origins, not every resource in an origin carries the same authority in the security sense of the word. An image is passive content and carries no authority, meaning it has no access to the objects and resources available to its origin. An HTML document carries the full authority of its origin, and scripts within it, or imported into it, can access every resource in that origin.

User agents decide how much authority to grant a resource by examining its media type. A resource served as image/png is treated as an image, and one served as text/html is treated as an HTML document. When hosting untrusted content, such as user-generated content, a web application can limit that content's authority by restricting its media type: serving it as image/png is less risky than serving it as text/html. Many web applications nevertheless put untrusted content into their HTML documents, and if that is not done carefully the application risks leaking its origin's authority to the untrusted content, a vulnerability commonly known as cross-site scripting.

The pitfall for new web platform features is to grant authority to resources irrespective of media type, because many applications serve untrusted content with restricted media types and a new feature that grants authority to those pieces of content introduces vulnerabilities into existing applications. The RFC's advice is to grant authority to media types that already have the origin's full authority, or to new media types designed specifically to carry the new authority. Some user agents also use content sniffing, treating content as if it had a different media type from the one the server supplied, in order to stay compatible with servers that supply incorrect types; if that is not done carefully, a user agent can end up granting an image the privileges of an HTML document.
sections.plainLanguage: Being in the same origin is not by itself permission to act. A picture has no rights, while a web page has the full rights of its site, and the browser tells them apart by the type of content the server says it is sending.

sections.title: What an Origin May Do
sections.content:
Most objects exposed by the user agent, which are also known as application programming interfaces, are available only to the same origin: content retrieved from one URI can access the objects associated with content from another URI if and only if the two belong to the same origin. There are exceptions, such as parts of HTML's Location interface, which are available across origins so that other browsing contexts can be navigated, and HTML's postMessage interface, which is visible across origins on purpose to make cross-origin communication possible. Exposing objects to foreign origins is dangerous and should be done only with great care.

Access to network resources depends on whether they are in the same origin as the content trying to reach them. Reading information from another origin is generally forbidden, but an origin is permitted to use some kinds of resource from others: it may execute scripts, render images and apply style sheets from any origin, and it may display content from another origin, such as an HTML document in a frame. A network resource can also opt in to being read by other origins, for example with Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, and in those cases access is typically granted per origin.

Sending information to another origin is permitted, though sending it in arbitrary formats is dangerous, so user agents restrict documents to particular protocols, such as an HTTP request without custom headers, and adding more allowed protocols must be done carefully.

Whenever a user agent allows one origin to interact with resources from another, it invites security issues: displaying images from another origin leaks their height and width, and allowing network requests to another origin gives rise to cross-site request forgery. Implementors often balance those risks against the benefits, since an HTML user agent that blocked cross-origin requests would prevent users from following hyperlinks. One pitfall is the temptation to grant a privilege to one resource while withholding it from another in the same origin; that is ineffective, because user agents do not isolate resources within an origin, so the resource without the privilege can usually obtain it anyway. Privileges should therefore be granted or withheld from origins as a whole.
sections.plainLanguage: Content can normally use the browser's programming interfaces and read data only within its own origin. It may still load scripts, images and styles from elsewhere, and it may send things anywhere, but the rules are narrow and each exception adds risk.

sections.title: Working Out the Origin of a URI
sections.content:
The RFC gives an algorithm for the origin of a URI. If the URI does not use a hierarchical element as a naming authority, or is not an absolute URI, the implementation generates a fresh globally unique identifier and returns that. Running the algorithm again for the same URI can produce a different value, so user agents typically compute the origin of a document once and use it for later security checks rather than recomputing it each time.

The scheme component is taken and converted to lowercase. If the implementation does not support the protocol given by that scheme, it again generates a fresh globally unique identifier. If the scheme is file, the implementation may return an implementation-defined value; the RFC notes that user agents have historically given file content a great deal of privilege, that granting all local files such wide privileges can lead to privilege escalation, and that using a globally unique identifier for each file URI is the most secure option.

The host component is converted to lower case using the i;ascii-casemap collation. The document assumes the user agent has already done IDNA processing, so the host will contain only LDH labels, because any non-ASCII labels have already been converted to their A-labels. That is why origin-based security policies are sensitive to the IDNA algorithm the user agent uses.

If the URI has no port component, the port is the default port for the protocol given by the scheme; otherwise it is the port component of the URI. The algorithm then returns the triple of scheme, host and port.
sections.plainLanguage: To find the origin of an address, take its scheme, host and port, put the scheme and host in lower case, and use the scheme's default port when the address does not name one. Addresses that are not absolute, or that use a scheme the browser does not support, get a fresh random identity instead, so that each one is alone.

sections.title: Writing an Origin as Text
sections.content:
The RFC defines two ways to serialize an origin, one to a Unicode string and one to an ASCII string. Both start the same way: if the origin is not a scheme, host and port triple, the result is the string null, that is the code point sequence U+006E, U+0075, U+006C, U+006C.

Otherwise the result starts with the scheme, then the string :// is appended. In the Unicode serialization, the host part is then appended, with its components separated by full stop characters; a component that is an A-label is replaced by the corresponding U-label, and any other component is used verbatim. In the ASCII serialization the host part is appended as it is.

Finally, if the port differs from the default port for the protocol given by the scheme, a colon and the port in base ten are appended. Otherwise no port appears.
sections.plainLanguage: An origin is written the way you would write the address itself, without a path, and without a port when it is the default one. Origins that are not a scheme, host and port are written as the word null.

sections.title: The HTTP Origin Header
sections.content:
The Origin header field has the syntax origin = "Origin:" OWS origin-list-or-null OWS, where origin-list-or-null is either the four characters null or a list of serialized origins separated by spaces, and a serialized origin is a scheme, then ://, then a host, and optionally a colon and a port.

When included in an HTTP request, the header indicates the origins that caused the user agent to issue the request, as defined by the API that triggered it. A user agent that runs scripts on behalf of origins may use the header to tell the server the security context in which the script was running when it caused the request. Sometimes more than one origin contributes to causing a request: if the request was first issued by one origin and later redirected by another, the user agent may list both.

The user agent may include an Origin header in any HTTP request, but it must not include more than one. Whenever it issues a request from a privacy-sensitive context it must send the value null. The document does not define what a privacy-sensitive context is; applications that generate HTTP requests can designate contexts as privacy-sensitive to impose restrictions on how the user agent generates the header. Each serialized origin must be the ASCII serialization of an origin, and no two consecutive serialized origins in the list can be identical, so the user agent must not generate a second one that repeats the first.
sections.plainLanguage: The header tells the server where the request came from, so the server can decide whether to answer. A request made from a context the page has marked as private reports the word null instead of a real origin.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The same-origin policy is one of the cornerstones of security for many user agents, including web browsers. Some user agents tried other models, such as taint tracking and exfiltration prevention, but those proved difficult to implement at the time. Evaluating the security of the policy is difficult because the origin concept plays such a central role, and the origin is just a unit of isolation, imperfect as most such notions are. The RFC then lists some systemic weaknesses.

The policy relies on the Domain Name System for security, because many commonly used URI schemes, such as http, use DNS-based naming authorities. If the DNS is partly or fully compromised, the policy may not give applications the security they need. Schemes such as https are more resistant, because user agents also use certificates to check where content came from, and schemes such as chrome-extension use a public-key naming authority and are fully secure against DNS compromise. Isolating content retrieved from different URI schemes is essential to containing the effects of a DNS compromise.

Many technologies in use, such as cookies, predate the modern origin concept and use different units of isolation, which leads to vulnerabilities. One alternative is to use only the registry-controlled domain, such as example.com rather than www.example.com, as the unit of isolation. The RFC says this is not recommended: the notion of a registry-controlled domain is a function of human practice around the DNS rather than a property of the DNS itself, since many municipalities run public registries deep in the hierarchy and the widely used public suffix lists are hard to keep up to date and vary between implementations; and the practice is incompatible with URI schemes that do not use a DNS-based naming authority, where the notion of a registry-controlled public key is incoherent, and with schemes such as nntp that use dotted delegation in the opposite direction.

On ambient authority, user agents grant authority to content based on its URI rather than on which objects the content can designate, and that separation can lead to vulnerabilities: if an attacker can inject script into an HTML document, those scripts run with the authority of the document's origin, perhaps giving them access to sensitive information such as the user's medical records. If the script's authority were limited to the objects it could designate, the attacker would gain nothing by injecting it.

Finally, the security properties of the policy can depend on details of the IDNA algorithm the user agent uses. A user agent might map some international domain names, those involving the U+00DF character for example, to different ASCII representations depending on whether it uses IDNA2003 or IDNA2008. Moving from one algorithm to another might redraw security boundaries, erecting new ones or, worse, tearing down the boundary between two entities that distrust each other, and changing boundaries is risky because combining two mutually distrusting entities into one origin might let one attack the other.
sections.plainLanguage: The origin rule rests on the domain name system and on the way non-English names are turned into ASCII, so a mistake in either can move the boundary between two sites and let one of them into the other.

items.title: Trust
items.text: Trust is expressed by URI: a document says which addresses it trusts for code and for data.

items.title: Origin
items.text: A protection domain made of the scheme, host and port.

items.title: Authority
items.text: Not everything in an origin has the same rights; the media type decides.

viz.caption: The grammar of the Origin header (Section 7.1)

data.title: Origin
data.code:
origin              = "Origin:" OWS origin-list-or-null OWS
origin-list-or-null = %x6E %x75 %x6C %x6C / origin-list
origin-list         = serialized-origin *( SP serialized-origin )
serialized-origin   = scheme "://" host [ ":" port ]
